Residual Compensation of Dynamic Asymmetric Ground Effect

Goal: land a multirotor UAV accurately on a laterally moving platform, such as a vehicle or a boat deck.
Ground effect is normally treated as a symmetric increase in thrust as a rotor nears a surface.
That model is adequate for hover over a static pad, but not for a descent onto a translating platform.
Two mechanisms break the left–right symmetry of the airflow and create a roll torque: rotor airspeed asymmetry and platform surface slip.
We name this combined disturbance dynamic asymmetric ground effect (DAGE).
Approach: keep a stable PID cascade and learn only the correction it is missing — a gated residual controller.
A 2026 survey of moving-platform landing reports that aerodynamic disturbances grow stronger and faster as platform speed rises.
Classical PID and SE(3) controllers assume nominal aerodynamics — an assumption that fails in the final metre of descent.
Model predictive control depends on an internal model that DAGE violates exactly where precision matters.
End-to-end reinforcement learning gives no stability guarantee outside its training distribution.
The disturbance does not vanish under perfect tracking: matching the platform means flying at its speed through still air.
Published learning results are often compared with weak baselines and tested on the same disturbance they were trained on.
Problem Statement:

When a multirotor descends onto a laterally moving platform, an altitude- and velocity-dependent roll torque appears that symmetric ground-effect models cannot predict, and classical controllers lose touchdown accuracy because of it.
Objectives:
1. Formalise DAGE through its two mechanisms — airspeed asymmetry and surface slip — and design a gated residual controller that cancels it while the PID cascade keeps authority.
2. Evaluate it fairly: against a tuned PID and a disturbance observer, on a disturbance field unseen in training, and test whether the state-space safety gate actually provides safety.
Nonlinear Flight Control — cascaded PID loops, geometric control on SE(3), input-to-state stability.
Rotor Aerodynamics — ground effect, wall-jet formation, advance-ratio asymmetry near a surface.
Residual Learning — learning only the additive correction to a fixed, stable base controller.
Machine Learning — multilayer perceptron regression over sliding state windows.
Out-of-Distribution Detection — distance gates, uncertainty estimation, safe policy adaptation.
Statistical Evaluation — Monte Carlo trials, Wilson score intervals, paired bootstrap tests.
Embedded Computing — running inference inside a 100 Hz flight-control loop.

slides.title: Literature Survey / Existing System

groups.text: Research Gap:
No existing model of the roll torque caused by platform translation; ground-effect work assumes a static surface.
Learned compensators are usually tested on the disturbance they were trained on, against weak PD baselines.
Safety gating is assumed to work, never tested: no study compares state-space gating with output-uncertainty gating.
Fast platforms remain unsolved, which is exactly where the disturbance is strongest.
Most validation is simulation-only or on static pads; moving-platform flight data is scarce.

groups.text: Gated residual architecture:
1. Nominal cascade — vertical PID, lateral outer loop and roll PID, with integral action.
2. Residual network — predicts the DAGE roll torque and the vertical lift anomaly.
3. Safety gate — scales the network output by a factor between 0 and 1.
4. Final command = nominal command − gate × network output; at gate 0 the loop is exactly the PID cascade.
5. Boundedness follows from an input-to-state-stability argument on the nominal loop.
Implementation:
Input: 40 ms sliding window of roll, roll rate, altitude, climb rate and commands (24 features).
Network: three hidden layers [64, 64, 32] with tanh activations; 7,906 parameters, NumPy only.
Training: 400 PID trajectories, platform speed 0–4 m/s, split by trajectory; validation MSE 0.0072.
Gate: per-feature standardised distance, threshold at the 99th percentile of training data.
Testing: reduced-order 100 Hz simulator, 500 randomised Monte Carlo trials per condition.

groups.text: First formal model of the roll disturbance created by platform translation, with its two physical mechanisms separated.
Shows the disturbance does not disappear under perfect tracking, so the problem is not self-solving.
Honest baselines: against PD the gain looks like 2.4% → 100%; against a tuned PID it is 80.8% → 100% — we report the second.
Tested on a disturbance field with different gains, decay and mechanism balance, so the result is not circular.
Negative result: the standard state-space safety gate never fires as calibrated, and hurts performance when forced to.
Explains why (self-masking) and supports gating on output uncertainty — the direction recent 2026 work also takes.
Landing-envelope success (500 trials per condition):
RMS roll at 3.0 m/s falls from 0.0291 to 0.0134 rad; roll violations at 5.0 m/s fall from 53.6% to 0%.
Inference cost is 7,744 multiply–accumulate operations per step, well inside a 100 Hz control budget.
Deliverables: an IEEE-format paper, a reproducible simulator and the full evaluation harness.
DAGE is a real and predictable disturbance: an altitude- and velocity-dependent roll torque from rotor airspeed asymmetry and platform surface slip.
The residual controller improves every touchdown metric at every nonzero platform speed and extrapolates usefully beyond its training range.
The safety gate, expected to be the most defensible component, proved the weakest: inert as calibrated and harmful when forced to fire.
Gating therefore belongs on the uncertainty of the residual output, not on input-space distance.
Limitation: results come from a reduced-order simulator, and the disturbance model remains a physically motivated hypothesis.
Next steps: full software-in-the-loop validation, then tethered flight tests over a moving ground vehicle.
Thank You
